issues.legal_issue: A municipal committee may exercise its power to control encroachments and sales on public streets without first making bye-laws governing the conditions and periods for permission.
material_facts: The vendors sold cooked food from stalls on public streets under temporary permissions.
The vendors argued that the committee could not stop the trade because it had made no bye-laws regulating permissions.
issues.conclusion: The absence of bye-laws did not prevent the committee from acting under its general power to grant or withdraw permission for use of public streets.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 173(1) and 188(u) of the Punjab Municipal Act, 1911, serve distinct purposes. Section 173(1) authorises permission for specified uses of public streets and allows that permission to be withdrawn; section 188(u) concerns bye-laws for regulating conditions and periods of permission in other contexts, such as temporary street uses for particular occasions or building work. The court held that section 188 was not designed to govern permanent street trading that could create unhygienic conditions.

predicates.municipal_street_trade_challenge: A person challenges a municipal authority's control of trade conducted on a public street.
predicates.street_goods_or_stalls_are_placed_on_a_p: A trader places goods for sale or a stall on a public street.
predicates.no_bylaws_regulate_the_permission: The municipality has not made bye-laws regulating the conditions or periods for the relevant permission.

issues.definition: When a person challenges municipal control of street trade involving goods or stalls on a public street, the municipality's power to control or withdraw permission is not defeated merely because it has made no bye-laws regulating that permission.

issues.legal_issue: Food-safety rules do not displace municipal power to prevent food sales on public streets where the restriction addresses street obstruction or insanitary conditions.
material_facts: The vendors sold cooked food on public streets.
The committee's resolution prohibited cooked-food sales because the trade created insanitary conditions and facilities necessary for minimum sanitation could not be provided.
The vendors argued that the food-adulteration legislation and rules occupied the field and displaced the committee's power.
issues.conclusion: The food-adulteration legislation did not prevent the committee from prohibiting street sales of cooked food to address obstruction or insanitary conditions.
issues.legal_principle: The Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954, including sections 23, 24 and 25, and the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules, 1955, including rule 50, address food purity and sanitary preparation, storage and sale. Those provisions override municipal rules or bye-laws only where they cover the same field. Section 173(1) of the Punjab Municipal Act, 1911, addresses the distinct concerns of obstruction on public streets and insanitary conditions in their neighbourhood.

predicates.municipal_street_trade_challenge: A person challenges a municipal authority's restriction on trade conducted on a public street.
predicates.cooked_food_is_sold_on_a_public_street: A trader sells cooked food from a public street.
predicates.municipal_restriction_addresses_obstruct: The municipality restricts the sale to address obstruction to street users or insanitary conditions in the neighbourhood.

issues.definition: When cooked food is sold on a public street and the municipality restricts the sale to address obstruction or insanitary conditions, food-safety rules do not displace the municipality's street-control power.

issues.legal_issue: A person has no fundamental right to conduct street trading in a manner that obstructs public passage or creates insanitary conditions, and a municipal authority may prohibit that trade to prevent those harms.
material_facts: The vendors conducted cooked-food businesses from stalls on public streets.
The committee found that cooked-food sales created insanitary conditions and could not be supported with facilities such as running water and sewer connections.
The committee passed a resolution banning the sale of cooked food on public streets, and the court found no bad faith or unreasonable exercise of its power.
issues.conclusion: The vendors had no fundamental right to conduct street trading in the manner at issue, and the committee could prohibit the trade under its street-control power.
issues.legal_principle: Section 173(1) of the Punjab Municipal Act, 1911, permits municipal action concerning street uses that obstruct public passage or create insanitary conditions. The right to pass and repass along a public street does not entail a fundamental right to trade there in a manner causing those harms. Roberts v. Hopwood, Pyx Granite Co. v. Ministry of Housing, C. S. S. Motor Service v. Madras State, and Westminster Corporation v. London and North Western Railway were considered but did not assist the vendors: the court found no ulterior purpose, bad faith or unreasonable action.

predicates.trader_uses_a_public_street: A trader conducts business from a public street.
predicates.trade_obstructs_public_passage_or_create: The trade obstructs people using the street or creates insanitary conditions in the neighbourhood.
predicates.municipal_action_is_not_badminded_or_unr: The municipality acts without bad faith or an unreasonable or ulterior purpose.

issues.definition: If a trader uses a public street and the trade obstructs public passage or creates insanitary conditions, the municipality may prohibit it when its action is not bad-minded or unreasonable.

issues.legal_issue: Failure to provide an alternative site does not establish unconstitutional discrimination where traders did not all apply for or receive alternative sites and the proposed sites were outside the municipal committee's jurisdiction.
material_facts: Some vendors were not allotted alternative sites, while others received or were considered for them.
Not all vendors applied for alternative sites or approved of the sites offered.
The proposed alternative sites were under the jurisdiction of another authority, not the municipal committee.
issues.conclusion: The absence of an alternative site for a particular vendor did not establish discrimination by the municipal committee.
issues.legal_principle: The court found no discrimination because the vendors were not similarly situated as to applications and acceptance of sites, and the municipal committee lacked jurisdiction over the proposed sites. The judgment did not identify a statutory provision or earlier case as the basis for this conclusion.
